```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "B names a concrete payer: engineering leads or CTOs paying as a team expense. A admits it has no defined payer and no evidence of any institutional buyer.",
    "B's price anchor is a direct competitor's published flat rate (apidrift.co at $29/mo). That sits above A's $8–20/mo consumer range, so a small number of paying orgs is enough to clear the 90-day goal.",
    "B's demand quotes describe recurring production incidents and customer-facing breakage, which is pain a business spends money to avoid. A's quotes describe personal benefit or a gap in generic chatbots, with no sign anyone would pay.",
    "B has a built-in billing and distribution route (GitHub Marketplace, free to list) suited to one operator. A depends on consumer app acquisition at $20–50 per user through ASO, which the brief itself says is hard to recoup at $8/mo.",
    "Both spaces are crowded with free options. A's free incumbents add credibility advantages (Stanford-backed Noora, SOC2-certified Yoodli with enterprise clients) plus professional skepticism from r/slp and health-claim risk. B's competitors are mostly visibly indie projects, which suggests a solo entrant can compete on a narrow wedge.",
    "B's task (watch, diff, scan, open PR) is well-bounded for agent automation. A's brief says its core is a commodity LLM wrapper with no evident moat."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's payer and pricing case rests entirely on Yoodli's published tiers. Yoodli is a different, enterprise-backed product. A's own price evidence for its closest consumer analog (Convo, ~$8) comes from a single user review with no official pricing page. The most persuasive demand quote is a testimonial curated on a competitor's marketing page. None of A's demand evidence shows willingness to pay.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. Both briefs show saturated markets with free competitors. B's demand quotes show pain but not proven willingness to pay for a third-party tool, three of B's competitors are free, and B carries real trust risk from false positives and from granting PR access to source code. One of B's channel sources was flagged by the brief for a prompt-injection attempt, so its CAC figure is directional only. B wins mainly because it has a defined business payer and a higher published price anchor, while A's payer is undefined."
}
```
